analysis.one_liner: Blocks most COVID-19 lawsuits against businesses, employers, and health care providers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors on December 2, 2020, referred to three House committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE TO WORK Act would have rewritten who can sue for coronavirus exposure or medical harm during the pandemic. Workers, customers, students, and patients would have had to prove by 'clear and convincing evidence' — a much higher bar than normal — that a business or health care provider was grossly negligent or acted willfully before any court case could proceed. It would also have capped damages, made people give up their right to a jury unless they signed up, limited class actions, narrowed federal workplace safety and anti-discrimination enforcement, and let employers escape WARN Act notice when mass layoffs were blamed on the pandemic.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, businesses, schools, nursing homes, and health care providers facing potential COVID-19 lawsuits; insurers who sell liability coverage; and large companies with the resources to meet the higher evidence standard and push cases into federal court. Small businesses get some protection too, but the bill's terms mostly help defendants who would otherwise face ordinary negligence suits.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the burden of proof to 'clear and convincing evidence' and requires proof of gross negligence or willful misconduct before any COVID exposure or medical liability suit can succeed, a far higher bar than ordinary negligence law [S2][S3].
Requires plaintiffs to plead every place and person visited in the 14 days before symptoms and to attach a non-treating expert affidavit and certified medical records just to file a case [S3].
Caps compensatory damages at economic losses, limits punitive damages, and lets defendants remove cases from state courts to federal courts, which tend to be less favorable to plaintiffs [S3].
Shields employers from enforcement under OSHA, the FLSA, Title VII, the ADA, ADEA, WARN, and GINA when they were 'generally following' government guidance during the pandemic [S3].

Amends the WARN Act so mass layoffs or hour reductions during the COVID emergency don't count as 'employment loss' triggering the 60-day advance notice workers normally get before plant closings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who get sick on the job, customers or students infected at a business or school, and patients harmed in hospitals or nursing homes — they would lose most practical routes to court. Taxpayers could also bear costs when injured people can't recover from the responsible party and instead rely on public programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick workers, customers, patients, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: A 'clear and convincing evidence' standard with a gross-negligence requirement would make it practically impossible to win even in cases where a business or nursing home's negligence clearly caused someone's infection and death [S2][S3].
Shielding employers from OSHA and Title VII enforcement based only on 'generally following' guidance could let unsafe conditions and discriminatory practices during the pandemic go unchallenged [S3].
Exempting pandemic-era layoffs from WARN Act notice would leave workers with no advance warning before plant closings or mass layoffs, removing time to plan or find new work [S3].
Class action opt-in requirements and MDL restrictions would make it nearly impossible to aggregate claims against a single company, shifting power to defendants [S3].
The bill would override stronger state tort and consumer protection laws, centralizing authority in federal courts and removing local democratic control over liability standards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There's a legitimate interest in not letting pandemic-era litigation bankrupt businesses that acted in good faith under rapidly changing guidance. But the bill's actual terms go far beyond shielding good-faith actors — it raises the bar so high and strips so many procedural tools that even strongly meritorious cases (e.g., a nursing home with no PPE causing dozens of deaths) would likely fail. The cost falls directly on sick and injured people, and it removes a key accountability tool that lets families and workers seek redress when safety rules are ignored.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary, Education and Labor, and Energy and Commerce Committees on December 2, 2020, and died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. James Comer introduced the bill on December 2, 2020, with no cosponsors listed at any point [S1][S4].
It was referred that same day to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce Committees [S5].
No further legislative action occurred — the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete, since the bill never advanced. Had it passed, employers, insurers, and health care providers would have been better off; the lack of action means ordinary people retained the pre-existing (limited) right to sue for pandemic-related harm.

for.name: Rep. James Comer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE TO WORK Act in the House and referred it to three committees

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Republican, sponsored the bill; no Democrats or additional Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: Would gain broad immunity from COVID-related lawsuits and reduced exposure under workplace safety and anti-discrimination laws. The cost falls on sick workers and customers who would lose their main route to compensation.
Would gain near-total immunity from medical liability suits related to COVID care, including nursing homes. Patients harmed by poor pandemic-era care would have almost no recourse.
Would face far fewer and smaller payouts on COVID-related claims, with the cost shifting to injured people and government programs.

The bill's own findings single out 'trial lawyers' as the threat it aims to curb; it would sharply limit contingency-fee litigation and class actions that are also the main tool for ordinary people to get compensation.
